A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, and their text, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison. Existing appendix material can be matched despite renumbering, including v1 Appendix B becoming v2 Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original expert assessments of 50 research documents, experiments with 480 synthetic plagiarism examples, and empirical clustering and classification analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original empirical results and adds analysis of PeerRead reviews, revised clustering and classification experiments, and another research-paper case study.

M1.justification: The main proposal-generation and SSAG procedures remain unchanged. For the supplementary diagnostic classifier, Section 6 replaces bag-of-words title features with sentence embeddings of titles plus abstracts. v2 also explicitly adapts proposal generation to produce title-and-abstract outputs for these analyses.

E1.justification: v2 adds plagiarism assessment through PeerRead reviews of human-written papers from ACL 2017, ICLR 2017, CoNLL 2016, and NeurIPS 2017; v1 used human-paper data for title-based diversity and classification analyses. Appendix B also adds an AI-generated ICLR 2025 workshop-paper case. The original twelve topics, 50-document expert study, and 480-example synthetic test set remain.

E2.justification: Section 6 adds GPT-4o-generated proposals alongside Claude 3.5 Sonnet proposals in the comparative diversity and human-versus-LLM classification experiments. GPT-4o already appeared elsewhere in v1, but not in these comparisons. The plagiarism-detector comparator set in Table 3 is unchanged.

E3.justification: The supplementary analyses change from titles to concatenated titles and abstracts, and classification changes from bag-of-words to sentence-transformer features while retaining the 60:40 split. v2 adds a GPT-4o condition with 2,019 samples alongside Claude's 2,370. The new PeerRead experiment introduces Claude 3.7 Sonnet review scoring, NeurIPS subsampling, and named-source requirements for scores 4–5.

E4.justification: v2 adds a human-paper plagiarism-rate proxy analysis and a workshop-paper case examining uncredited overlap that escaped reviewing and automated checks. It also substantially revises the retained diversity and origin-classification probes through richer text inputs and an additional generator. The earlier case studies and synthetic detection example remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for these experiments. v2's description of human-paper rates as significantly lower does not introduce a documented statistical test.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 retain their results, including 24% verified plagiarism. New Table 4 reports human-paper proxy rates of 0.8% for ACL, 6.3% for ICLR, 5.3% for CoNLL, and 1.8% for NeurIPS. Section 6 replaces the title-only spread ratio of 0.76 and classification accuracy of 94.2% with title-and-abstract ratios of 0.81/0.72 and accuracies of 93.9%/92.6% for Claude/GPT-4o. These use changed conditions, not directly comparable performance updates. Appendix B adds an estimated similarity score of 3 or 4.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The regularization expression discussed in v2 Appendix B identifies overlap with cited work; it does not introduce a new mathematical definition, derivation, or theorem.

C1.justification: The abstract adds the claim that another 32% of ideas partially overlap with prior work and few are completely original, drawing on results already in v1 Table 2. The introduction extends its exemplar claim to AI-Scientist-v2 while qualifying the finding as plagiarism or substantial similarity. The central plagiarism and detector-inadequacy claims remain.

C2.justification: Section 6 newly interprets review-derived human-paper rates as evidence that LLM research has substantially higher plagiarism rates, although it describes the human analysis as a proxy rather than an equivalent expert study. Appendix B adds an explanation involving borrowed regularization applied to an unsuitable domain. The obsolete title-only limitations paragraph is removed, with title-and-abstract scope qualifications retained in Section 6.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the PeerRead analysis prompt in Table 11, documents the supplementary generation format and model-specific sample totals, and clarifies the allocation and overlap of the existing 13 experts. It replaces the anonymous code/results repository address with a named GitHub repository. Existing expert instructions, synthetic-generation prompt, and OpenScholar prompt are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to PeerRead, AI-Scientist-v2, Krueger and Memisevic's activation-stabilization work, and Jonschkowski and Brock's robotic-priors work. These support the new dataset analysis and workshop case. The broader related-work discussion and first-systematic-study positioning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized prose clarifications, expands the abstract and discussion, reorders discussion topics, and places Conclusion before Limitations. Appendix headings and cross-references are updated around the new case study. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 4 for human-paper rates and Table 11 for the review-analysis prompt. Figure 3 is redrawn for title-and-abstract embeddings, changing the plotted points, axis ranges, legend, and caption. Other figures and tables are retained, with subsequent tables renumbered and some layout reflow.

improvement.justification: The richer title-and-abstract analyses across two generators and the corroborated workshop-paper overlap case strengthen the supporting evidence while preserving the main results. However, Section 6 introduces a consequential human–LLM plagiarism-rate claim based on unequal detection procedures: extracting concerns from existing reviews versus directing experts to search actively for plagiarism. Table 11 also assigns incomplete reviews the lowest score. The PDFs do not validate this proxy comparison, so the evidential gains and new inferential weakness prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
